It is associated with "tangles," which show the MAP2 protein and abnormal forms of tau protein, as well as the presence of amyloid angiopathy and typical plaques, and symptoms include aphasia and progressive disorientation, indicating cortical dysfunction. Patients rarely become symptomatic before 50 years of age. But within the following 30 years up to 40% of the populace starts suffering from this disease. Name this degenerative neurological disorder, the most common cause of dementia in the elderly.

A more advanced form of it exhibits sigmoid behavior and is named for Goldbeter and Koshland. The Hill formula is preferred as an alternative to it since it cannot be used to describe behavior in instances of cooperative binding. Among the graphical depictions of it are the Hanes type, which is the most accurate, and the Eadie-Hofstee, which best shows bad measurements. However, in the lab it is most often represented by a linear double reciprocal or Lineweaver-Burke plot. Among the constants it utilizes are the namesake, better known as Km, and Vmax. Illustrating in mathematical terms the relationship between initial reaction velocity and substrate concentration, name this equation of enzyme kinematics.

This process may be more common in bacteria than in eukaryotes, where it occurs through horizontal gene transfer. One example of this process can be found on Santa Cruz Island among the Medium gound Finch population, whose beaks tend to conform to two different sized ideals, while those with intermediate beaks are selected against. One mechanism proposed to account for this process suggests that, given a particular environment, homozygous individuals may have greater fitness than heterozygous individuals for a certain trait. This model, known as disruptive selection, was first put forward by John Maynard Smith. Name this process whereby speciation may occur without the original species leaving its environment, often contrasted to the allopatric variety.

In the 1980's, Hoechst Celanese developed an improvement of this process which involved the use of lithium iodide, known as "low water" form of this process. It is similar to a newer, more environmentally friendly process which uses an iridium catalyst as opposed to the rhodium catalyst, the Cativa process. That rhodium based catalyst is a complex consisting of two carbonyl and two iodine ligands which sees the oxidative addition of methyl iodide derived from methanol, thus this reaction can be seen simply as a reaction between carbon monoxide and methanol. Identify this process that synthesizes a compound with formula CH3COOH, acetic acid.

One possible use of this mineral is the sequestering of CO2 from the atmosphere. At higher temperatures and pressures it undergoes a phase transition to wadsleyite, which can then undergo a further transition to ringwoodite. Thought to be the most abundant mineral in the Earth's mantle at shallower depths, it occurs in both mafic and ultramafic igneous rocks. Compostitions of this mineral are usually given as molar percentages of forsterite, the magnesium rich variety, and fayalite. Also giving its name to a group which includes tephroite, monticellite, and kirschsteinite, this is, what mineral also known as peridot and which occupies the top of the discontinuous branch of Bowen's reaction series.

Donald Mathews argued that this period integrated people into small, cohesive groups in his article " as an organizing process." One figure in this period introduced the "anxious bench," and promoted the idea that people were "moral free agents." Barton Stone and Thomas Campbell led the Restoration Movement during this period, which was sparked by men like James McGready and a large meeting at Cane Ridge. Theodore Weld and Lyman Beecher led regional movements during this period, which also featured Charles Finney holding revivals in the "burned-over district" of New York. During this period, Methodism became the largest religious denomination in the United States. Name this large-scale American religious movement that occurred in the first half of the nineteenth century.

One common way to synthesize these compounds is through the Prilezhaev reaction, which involves the use of m-CPBA. This reaction proceeds in a concerted step, via the butterfly mechanism. Another way to generate these is through the Johnson-Corey-Chaykovsky reaction, which involves their formation from carbonyl groups and sulfonium ylides. In an acidic solution, these compounds can undergo ring opening to form diols, while the most general way to make these involves reacting an alkene with a peroxyacid. Also known as oxiranes, what are these three-membered cyclic ethers?

A decrease in cytoplasmic pH causes the protonation of a histidine residue in the arginine-rich loop D of this class of proteins. The lack of Colton antigens is a marker for deficiency of one protein in this family, and the major intrinsic protein of the lens is sometimes referred to as number zero of this family. Knocking out number nine of this family was shown to improve survival after malarial infection by the man who discovered this family, Peter Agre. The best-known members of this family are number one, which maintains red blood cell osmotic pressure, and number two, whose expression is upregulated by ADH and which is found in the collecting duct of the kidney. Name these protein channels through which water passes.

The Havriliak-Negami relation adds exponential alpha and beta terms for asymmetry and broadening of spectra to one model named for this man, and if beta equals one, then it becomes the Cole-Cole equation. That model uses a term of one plus i times a field's frequency times the relaxation time to calculate the complex permittivity. When the ion term is dropped, the square root of the permittivity times the temperature of the electrons over the electron density times the squared charge is equal to one quantity named for this man in plasmas. Using a Taylor series to linearize the Poisson-Boltzmann equation gives rise to an equation partially named for this man, which states that the valence factor times the ionic strength is equal to the natural logarithm of the activity coefficient. Name this man, who names an equation alongside Huckel and whose namesake length is used to describe the screening out of electric fields.

An anharmonic oscillator exploiting this effect as a microelectromechanical system component was proposed by Serry, Walliser, and Maclay. Julian Schwinger has postulated that sonoluminescence arises due to this effect, and this effect requires that bag radius and mass are independent under a combination of the Skyrmion and MIT models, the chiral bag model of the nucleon. One setup for measuring it attached a polystyrene sphere to an atomic force microscope, and Lamoreaux used a torsional pendulum to achieve the first precise measurements of this effect. This force may produce pressures as large as an atmosphere at a separation of ten nanometers. Name this effect arising from zero-point energy, described by the attraction or repulsion due to virtual photons between two close uncharged metallic sheets in a vacuum.

One of these compounds is administered after testicular torsion to decrease the risk of infertility, and cradle cap, or seborrheic dermatitis, may be alleviated by the administration of another of these compounds. That second one possesses a valeric acid group, while the first is phosphorylated, cysteinated, decarboxylated, adenylylated, and phosphorylated again in coenzyme A synthesis, in which form it is usually found in food..Another of these compounds is prescribed to alleviate nausea during pregnancy, and is required for tryptophan metabolism and the production of red blood cells. Two of these compounds are essential cofactors that play roles in electron transport in the forms of FADH2 and NADH. Name this group of compounds, which include pyridoxine, cyanocobalamin, thiamine, riboflavin, and niacin, nine vitamins which are nonetheless numbered up to twelve.

Franco, Tenorio-Tagle, and Bodenheimer found that the production of this material propagates outward exponentially, and a critical value of three halves characterizes the exponential "w" factor of expansion; for values exceeding the critical value of "w," this material is produced supersonically in the so-called "champagne phase." Around class O and B stars, the cloud of this material is known as the Stromgren Sphere. Areas in which this material abounds can contain Bok Globules. Its presence characterizes the evolution of a GMC to a type of region named for this material, and the Lyman Alpha line is produced when this material recombines with free electrons. This material names the regions such as the Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula in which star formation occurs. Name this material that astronomers dub "H two," the charged form of the simplest element.

A sextet forming in this technique applied to Al49Fe30Cu21 indicates the transition to a superspin glass. The conversion electron type of this technique is used to study uranium-iron multilayers. Unlike in NMR, the relative height of split peaks in this technique depends on the angle between incident radiation and nuclear spin moment, and different wavelengths are scanned not by varying the strength of a magnetic field but via natural molecular vibrations and the consequent Doppler effect. This technique's namesake co-names a factor with Lamb often called the elastic incoherent structure factor, and a form of this technique was used to reveal the presence of a gravitational blueshift by Pound and Rebka. Name this analytic technique that relies on its namesake effect to ensure that some fraction of radiation has lost no energy due to recoil, allowing for proper resolution of the chemical environment of the target using nice, sharp gamma ray lines.

The gastrointestinal parasite Entamoeba histolytica can cause persistent diarrhea by secreting high levels of this molecule, and symptoms of cardiac fibrosis in East Africans can be related to high levels of this molecule in the Matoki variety of banana. The overstimulation of the 2B form of the receptor for this molecule can lead to retroperitoneal fibrosis, and the vast majority of the body's supply of this molecule is found in the enterochromaffin cells. Proteins that regulate levels of this molecule include p11, and its breakdown can lead to the formation of 5-HIAA. Controlled by the 5-HT receptors, DDC and TPH catalyze the synthesis of this chemical, low levels of which correspond to intense religious experience and defective signaling of which can lead to SIDS. Name this neurotransmitter synthesized from tryptophan, which can be selectively reuptaken in a treatment for depression.

One reaction named after this man usually uses a stream of nitrogen gas to carry one product to a chilled receiver, and it can only proceed if a certain intermediate contains at least one beta-hydrogen. Another reaction named after this chemist has an Oxy- variety that has an enolate intermediate and proceeds up to 1017 times faster than the standard version; that reaction produces anti-3,4 diastereomers when starting with the E,E or Z,Z variety of a certain reactant. The aforementioned reactions produce, respectively, anti-Zaitsev alkenes after heating tertiary amine oxides to 150 degrees and regioisomeric isomers of the original 1,5-dienes; the latter is complementary to the Hoffman elimination. Name this American chemist, the namesake of an [3, 3]-sigmatropic rearrangement and elimination.

One named for Martin and Puplett can determine differences in power while the Elitzur-Vaidman bomb testing experiment, which separates live bombs from duds, uses on these named for Mach and Zehnder. Fabry-Perot cavities are used in modern n-waves types which have largely replaced the older type developed by Jules Jamin. The most common type uses the relationship that distance is equal to one half the wavelength multiplied by the number of fringes. Identify these devices which includes one that contains a light source, a detector, and a half silver mirror to split light, notable for disproving the existence of the luminiferous aether in the Michelson-Morley experiment.

The alphabet of this language was responsible for the Romanization of Japanese hiragana that modernly begins with the consonant "h," using an "f" instead. The Nippo Jisho was a Japanese dictionary that translated words into this language. The consonants of "l" and "n" in this language were elided out when they were in between in vowels. The u's in this language are silent when combined with a "g" or "u," and the presence of an "m" or "n" in this language indicates a nasalization. This language's digraph "nh" is possibly a nasal glide, as evidenced by its usage for epenthesis. Places like Kristang and Daman speak a creole pidgin language whose vocabulary was derived from it, and along with Spanish, this Romance language influenced the Papiamento syntactically. This language also names a subfamily along with Galician that includes Fala Language and Leonese. Name this language used in Macao, Guinnea-Bissau, and its namesake country with capital at Lisbon.

As adults, one order in this taxonomic group consists entirely of an externa. In addition to Rhizocephala, it also contains the extinct order Lipostraca, which consists of only one species, Lepidocaris rhyniensis, thought to be the ancestor of order Anostraca. Although most species in this group excrete using green glands located near the antennae and maxillae, coxal glands are used by the sole surviving member of order Xiphosura. The last segment of the tail in this group is known as the telson, and most members of this group begin life as nauplius larvae. They are distinguished from other arthropods by the presence of a second pair of antennae, and the most well- known members of this group are in order Decapoda. Name this subphylum that includes crabs and lobsters.

In a modified form of this reaction, diethyl ether is used in the synthesis of cholestane. Other more notable modifications of this reaction include one that uses formic acid and ethanol to produce aryl alkenes and one that uses toluene in the Martin modification. One proposed mechanism uses a carbenoid intermediate, although it is agreed this reaction uses electrons supplied by the oxidation of a metal. It is analogous to another reaction run under basic conditions which can modified in a one pot process named after Huang and Minlon. Identify this chemical reaction which uses zinc amalgam and hydrochloric acid and, like the Wolff-Kishner reduction, reduces aldehydes or ketones to alkanes.

If you're a scientist who studies these phenomena, you probably know all about how to model their nucleation using the Discrete Element Method software ESyS Particle. One version of these phenomena is the subject of a landmark 1996 paper by Janusza that introduces "anticrack theory" as a means of understanding how the alpha-gamma phase transformation of olivine to spinel causes them. Amos Nur introduced the idea of a "storm" of these phenomena, and when they recur repeatedly, it is known as a "swarm" of them. In a subduction zone, the area where these phenomena are concentrated at low depths is known as the Wadati-Benioff Zone, which is home to the "deep focus" type. They also produce an acoustic Rayleigh wave and a horizontal shear Love wave, and they create waves that were used to locate the Gutenberg and Moho discontinuities. Name these P- and S-wave making phenomena, the magnitude of which can be measured using the Modified Mercalli or Richter scales.

One protein found on the membrane of this structure is Ire1, whose dimeric form is an endonuclease that splices Hac1 mRNA. Hereditary emphysema is caused by the aggregation of alpha-one-antitrypsin in this structure. Proteins destined for this structure typically contain a hydrophobic N-terminal signal sequence. Pro-alpha-six-integrin may be retained in this structure due to the lectin calnexin, a type I transmembrane protein. Protein disulfide isomerase catalyzes spontaneous disulfide bond formation in this structure, the only eukaryotic cell structure in which it can happen. Like the Golgi body, it may consist of a series of flattened disks known as cisternae. Name this organelle that synthesizes phospholipids and fats in its "smooth" variety and proteins in the ribosomes attached to its "rough" variety.

This equation can be derived by first taking Legendre transforms of internal energy, then using Euler's homogenous function theorem, and then taking a differential. It can also be derived by substituting Maxwell's thermodynamic relations after taking the full differential of a certain quantity. One side of this equation is written as a series of the number of components in the system and for a binary, isochoric and isothermic system, this equation reduces to a relationship between the number of moles of each component. Identify this equation that relates the change in chemical potential to changes in pressure and temperature, named for a French physicist and chemist from Yale.

This law is satisfied by perfectly aligned diffraction patterns in Ewald's sphere. Wave vectors ending on Wigner-Seitz cells will also satisfy this law. The same method used for finding Wigner-Seitz cells in Bravais lattices is used for finding the set of points, in k-space which can be reached from the origin without violating this law, known as Brillouin zones. This law is reduced from three primitive vectors noted as a, b, and c being multiplied by delta k or the scattering vector in three equations known as the Laue equations. This law states that the order number multiplied by wavelength equals two multiplied by the spacing distance between atomic lattices multiplied by the sine of the angle between the incident ray and the scattering plane. Name this law which states that an electric cloud moves when an atom is hit by X-rays.

A mixture of this compound's main components was found to be effective in situ when reacting with butylcyclohexanone. One synthesis of this product uses a compound named for Petasis. For it to be activated it must reacted with a base, typically pyridine, to generate a compound that contains a double bonded methylene known as a Schrock carbene. It then undergoes a [2+2] and a retro [2+2] cycloaddition reaction with the compound it modifies. It consists of a central methylene bonded to two metals, one of which is bonded to two cyclopentadienyl groups while the other one is bonded to two methyl groups. Identify this reagent that methylenates carbonyl groups and contains both aluminum and titanium.

Myringitis bullosa is a disease characterized by formation of blebs on this structure. It is divided into two parts, one of which is also known as Shrapnel's part, which lies next to the notch of Rivinus. Its medial surface is innervated by Jacobson's nerve, which is a branch of the ninth cranial nerve. Of the two subdivisions – the pars flaccida and the pars tensa – the latter is characterized by a cone of light in its anteroinferior quadrant. It can be ruptured by fracture of the temporal bone or by fluid column pressure and is semi-transparent allowing such things as the long process of the incus to be seen through it. Name this membrane that divides the external acoustic canal from the middle ear, and which is commonly known as the ear drum.

CeNA oligonucleotides are characterized by the presence of this compound, which can be added by syringe to Wilkinson's catalyst to form an addition product. This compound's ketone derivative is produced in the aldol condensation step of the Robinson annulations and can be synthesized from phenol in a variant of the Birch reduction. Like a similar compound with one fewer double bond, it may be used in the synthesis of adipic acid. It is typically synthesized in beginner chemistry labs by dehydrating a closely related alcohol compound with a phosphoric or sulfuric acid catalyst and it is also the final product in a reaction that prefers an endo product. Identify this compound that results from the reaction of 1,3 butadiene and ethane in the Diels-Alder, a six carbon ring with one double bond.

In both Stickler syndrome and sulphite oxidase deficiency it can be found ectopically. In homocystinuria and Marfan's syndrome it is commonly displaced downwards and upwards respectively. The Zonules of Zinn are its namesake suspensory ligaments which act to keep it in position. Though not related to the knee, it resides in a depression known as the patellar fossa. It is said to reside in the anterior segment of the larger structure to which it belongs and is situated directly anterior to the vitreous humor. It is covered entirely by a capsule, which conforms to its typical biconvex shape. Name this transparent structure that provides about 1/3 of the refractive power of the eye.

A special case of these allowing for easier insertions and deletions introduce "up-in" and "up-out" requests and is known as the relaxed type of them. All 3-nodes have a certain restriction in the "Left Leaning" type of these data structures, which maintain a one-to-one correspondence with a 2-3-4 tree. Deletion of nodes in these objects can be performed in a maximum of three rotations, and all of their leaf nodes contain no information. In these data structures, a simple path from one node to all of its descendants must contain the same number of nodes that share a property with the root of the tree. Like an AVL Tree, it provides a practical runtime of Big O of log n time for insertions, deletions and searches. Identify this type of self-balancing binary search tree, where every node is one of the two namesake colors.

The last two are also known by the names of Fletcher and Fitzgerald respectively, after the names of their discoverers. The other names associated with them include Stuart and Hageman, which denote the 10th and 12th ones. Absence of the 9th gives rise to Christmas disease, and the only element among their number is Calcium, which is required for activation of many of the others. Four of them can only be synthesized in the presence of vitamin K, and they can be activated by either the intrinsic or extrinsic pathways. Including mostly proteins such as fibrinogen and prothrombin, name these substances, which as their name suggests, partake in the coagulation of blood.

This scientist's most noted experiment created a two-dimensional electron gas in an inversion layer below a silicon dioxide MOSFET. This scientist discovered an effect whereby the factor "v" is consistent with the action of degenerate Landau levels, in contrast to an effect discovered by Robert Laughlin that relies on "quasiparticles" called anyons to explain fractional values for the filling factor. He also names a value that is equal to Planck's constant over the charge of the electron squared, and is measured in ohms. That constant named for this man, denoted R-sub-K, is the amount by which the resistance to a certain effect is quantized. Name this man who discovered a series of stepwise jumps in resistance at low temperatures, a result known as the Integer Quantum Hall Effect.

In Sikhism it can be divided into two types, with Arbuda and Sanjiva being the best examples. In Smritis, or Hindu legal texts, up to 21 types of it have been mentioned, though the only Hindu religious texts to describe it are the Puranas. Buddhism, like Sikhism and Hinduism, also gives it the name of Naraka. The tree of Zaqqum is present in the Islamic version known as Jahannam, whose name is derived from the Hebrew word connoting the same thing. In Norse myth, it is the site of Eljudnir, is encircled by the impassable river Gjoll, and is ruled by the youngest child of Angrboda and Loki. Perhaps better known is the Jewish version of Gehenna. FTP, name this common place, which according to Dante is home to nine circles.

A similar statement named partly for Huang Kun takes into account non- adiabatic terms, although the parameters behind this statement are considered adiabatic since one component is assumed to not have a finite relaxation time. It names a surface that describe nuclear dynamics governed by a time dependent Schrodinger equation, while its second step uses Eckart conditions to separate various forms of nuclear motion. This statement is supported by the fact that the electron to nuclear mass ratio is about 1/1800, but breaks down in the case of degenerate electronic energy levels. Identify this approximation that gives the total molecular wavefunction as the product of nuclear and electronic components, named for an American and German physicist.

This man is the first namesake of a linear partial differential equation that is elliptic or hyperbolic for negative or positive values of the Tchaplyguine variable. In addition to that equation for transonic flow partially named for Tricomi, this man lends his name to a criterion that can be used to calculate Legendre symbols. One of this man's theorems states that the operator x dot grad returns n times f of x when applied to a smooth function f of x that is homogeneous of degree n. This man's namesake fluid description uses a frame that is fixed in space, as opposed to the Lagrangian description. Carmichael's theorem generalizes a theorem due to this man that involves this man's namesake totient function. FTP name this solver of the bridges of Königsberg problem whose namesake number is the base of the natural logarithm.

The phase shift acquired by the Aharanov-Bohm effect for two identical charged particles traveling different paths is given by two pi times this quantity times the charge over Planck's constant. Molecular clouds undergo dynamic collapse on a modified Jeans length when the ratio of mass to this quantity reaches a critical value. The quantum of this quantity is given by Planck's constant over twice the electron charge, and is the inverse of the Josephson constant. The negative time derivative of this quantity equals the emf induced in a circuit according to Faraday's law. FTP, name this quantity which equals the integral of the magnetic field over any surface bounded by a particular closed loop.

They are exemplified in a reaction that uses a strong Bronsted or Lewis acid to convert divinyl ketones to a form of pentenone. Taking into account frontier orbitals, they classify certain systems as "symmetry allowed" and are supported by extended Huckel theory. They note that the reaction of compounds containing 4n+2 pi electrons will be a disrotatory process, while those containing 4n pi electrons will undergo a conrotatory process. This can be seen in the reaction of butadiene to cyclobutene, an electrocyclic process. Identify this set of rules used for predicting the stereochemistry of pericyclic reactions.

Population imbalance in a Fermi mixture leads to the breakdown of this property at the Chandrasekhar-Clogston limit. The ability of one material to display this property was discovered by Lee, Osheroff, and Richardson when they were experimenting with that material's negative heat of solidification below.3 K. In thin layers, materials with this property adsorb to a surface because of van der Waals interactions, and undergo wave motion dubbed "third sound." Materials with this property can produce a Rollin film and undergo the Onnes effect. Quantum sound waves are responsible for this property according to Landau's theory of it. Name this property that exists below the lambda point in helium-four, when a liquid's viscosity becomes zero and there is no resistance to flow.

The complete description of this quantum mechanical system includes a term proportional to a Dirac delata function of position called the Darwin term. The angular portions of the wave functions that describe this system are proportional to terms given by the Rodrigues relation, the Laguerre polynomials, and a radiative correction known as the Lamb shift was discovered in this system. The spin-flip transition corresponding to 1420 megahertz in this quantum mechanical system is widely used in radio astronomy, arises from hyperfine splitting, and is called the 21-centimeter line, while another transition in this system that is useful in astronomy gives rise to the Lyman- alpha forest. With transition energies given by the Rydberg formula with Z equal to 1, identify this system that also exhibits the Balmer and Paschen series and consists of a single electron bound to a single proton.

Bromine in methanol and dilute sulfuric acid are used to convert the alcohol of this compound to a dihydropyran in the Achmatowicz reaction. An "interrupted" modification of one reaction that produces this compound involves quinine in the presence of a proton sponge, and that reaction is catalyzed by amines and involves alpha-halogen ketones and beta-dicarbonyl compounds and is the Feist-Benary synthesis. 1,4-diketones are reacted with phosphorus pentoxide to produce these in Paal-Knorr synthesis, and these compounds are hydrogenated with a palladium catalyst to produce the "tetrahydro" variety of ether. Analogous to thiophene and pyrrhole, name this aromatic compound with a five-element ring containing one oxygen atom.

In Germanic folklore, a giant named Lars Krands used one of these objects to transport sand that he then dumped on an offending farmer. In the Aeneid, Entellus uses one of these objects to kill a bull after defeating Dares in a contest. In the Mabinogion, Manawyddan uses one of these objects to store a captive mouse which he intends to hang for stealing grain from him. In Norse myth, one of these objects belonging to the giant Skrymir is mistaken by Thor for a house during a journey to the realm of Utgard-Loki. King Amycus, who attempted to impede the progress of the Argonauts before being defeated by Polydeuces, owned some of these objects that had spikes concealed in them, and Thor owned some iron examples of these objects, which were borrowed from the giantess Grith, and which he used to kill the giant Geirrod by throwing a piece of iron at him. Identify these objects, one of which had to be worn on Thor's right hand in order to wield Mjolnir and which might be useful to boxers.

Dekker's algorithm was the first to successfully apply these constructs, and Peterson's algorithm, which implements a bounded waiting scheme, also makes use of these constructs and was generalized to n greater than 2 my Hofri. These constructs usually support two operations denoted V and P, which correspond to an increment and a decrement operation, and the blocked-queue implementation of these constructs keeps track of the next action to be invoked through a first-in-first-out mechanism. Usually used to solve common classes of problems like the producer-consumer problem, incorrect use of these constructs can lead to either starvation or a condition in which no processes are making progress, deadlock. Invented by Edsger Dijkstra as a solution to the "dining philosophers" problem, identify these programming constructs which control access to shared resources between processes.

Two proteins associated with this structure assist in the transport of glucosinolate into plant cells as an antifungal defense, and one analogue of this structure seals septal pores in several filamentous ascomycetes and is called the Woronin body. In plants, the components of the ascorbate- glutathione cycle are produced in this structure, and one defect in it leads to a disorder characterized by high levels of pipecolic acid, which is related to another disease of this structure results from the alpha-oxidation of phytanic acid. Both Refsum disease and adrenoleukodystrophy fall in the Zellweger spectrum of diseases affecting this organelle, which as a result compromises the myelin sheath. This organelle produces the manganese form of superoxide dismutase and uric acid oxidase, but is best known for producing catalase. Name this organelle that produces enzymes that break down peroxides.

These objects were the subject of Otto Struve's Algol paradox, which was resolved by Gerard Kuiper, and a recent class of these systems to be discovered is the class of cataclysmic variables. Methods of detecting these systems include visual, spectroscopic, and eclipsing methods, as well as detections of instances of common proper motion, and the orbital periods of these systems provide the most direct and precise way of measuring solar masses. These systems usually undergo mass transfer between components through the first Lagrange point once one half has filled its Roche lobe, and examples include systems like the Hulse-Taylor system, whose decaying period provides evidence for gravitational waves, and the Xi Ursae Majoris system, the first for which orbital ellipticity was established. Also including systems like the one containing Castor and Pollux, identify these systems that consist of two stars gravitationally bound to each other.
